prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength combine the accuracy of single-ion clocks with the statistics of many atoms, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B030 alone, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Reading the full first round, the case has become more specific rather than stronger in volume. The new idea is the magic-wavelength lattice: a wavelength at which the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so that Doppler and recoil effects are suppressed while thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at once. That is what separates this work from a comb, which is a ruler, and from a single-ion clock, which is one absorber. The scientific content that followed, namely forbidden-transition physics, blackbody-shift control, collisional and many-body shifts at high density, and agreement at about 1e-18 between laboratories in Japan, the US and Europe, is demonstrated and not prospective. The one-sentence answer to the chair's first question is: the 2005 prize honoured the optical frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is a many-atom neutral system whose magic-wavelength trapping removes the usual trade-off between ensemble statistics and single-ion accuracy. The case rests on measured performance, not on the redefinition of the second. I ranked it first at the opening for physical reasons, and the fact that several colleagues moved to it does not enter my judgement beyond showing that its credit and maturity survive scrutiny from outside atomic physics.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection is the one I take most seriously, and Mehlig is right that the 2005 and 2012 citations share methods (laser spectroscopy, cooling and trapping) with the lattice clock, so the overlap is a matter of degree and the citation must carry the burden of showing what is new. I would therefore not accept the bare wording 'optical lattice clocks' or wording about timekeeping in general; the citation should name the trapped neutral atoms and the combination of accuracy and statistics. Attribution remains a judgement. Kroll is right that I should not dismiss the Boulder systematic evaluations, and I still would not name Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow or the ion-clock groups: they carried the field forward but the proposal and its leading realization sit with the two names. If an expert in metrology showed that another group demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock independently and earlier than Katori, I would reconsider the pair. A residual weakness is that the committee cannot yet say the clock has changed the SI second, so the argument must stay with what was measured.

responses.point: Mehlig agrees on the science and the two-person credit but does not treat the 2005 and 2012 overlap as closed, because the methods are close, and asks that the citation emphasise neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength in large ensembles.
responses.response: I accept that, and it changes my wording. In round 1 my citation spoke of a route to timekeeping at the 10^-18 level, which is the framing most exposed to your objection because precision time is exactly what the earlier prizes touched. The new citation names the trapped neutral atoms and the magic wavelength. I do not agree that the methods being near means the achievements coincide. Cooling and trapping are shared tools, but the cancellation of the lattice light shift on a narrow clock transition is a separate idea, and without it neither the many-atom statistics nor the 1e-18 systematic control exists. If the overlap still leaves you uneasy after this wording, I would like to know which element of the citation you think is already covered.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B030 up from sixth because the physics is the achievement, but asks that the citation say what the clocks have enabled so that the overlap objection does not stay open, and keeps B020 as first alternative.
responses.response: I agree that a citation should say why the work matters and not only what was built, but I would anchor it in the invention's own content, the accuracy-with-statistics combination, rather than list applications such as dark matter searches that are still being pursued. Redshift tests at millimetre scale and bounds on varying constants are consequences already demonstrated or in progress, and I am happy for the committee's public text to mention them, though I would keep them out of the citation to avoid overclaiming. I also note that IceCube is not a competing configuration for me yet: the case for the neutrino window is real, but I cannot defend a particular three-name split among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, and you and Pearce still differ on the third name.

responses.point: Kroll says the Boulder effort drove the evaluation to the 1e-18 level and into the many-body regime, so dropping either Katori or Ye would misstate the history, and that the award should be for the lattice-clock concept and its realization and not optical clocks in general.
responses.response: I agree with both points and they sharpen my own position. I had put the weight on Katori's proposal and early demonstrations, and your point about the systematic evaluation at Boulder is correct: accuracy at 1e-18 is a physics result about blackbody, collisional and many-body shifts and not a refinement of the concept. I also take your caution about performance records. The citation should honour the invention and its realization and not a sequence of record uncertainties, which is why I want the magic-wavelength mechanism rather than only the 10^-18 number in the text. I do not think either name can be dropped, and I would not add a third.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, accepts that the lattice clock is a different invention from the 2005 and 2012 work, wants the citation built around the invention and its accuracy and not around the redefinition, and says B020 would be his reversion if its attribution gap proved smaller than he judges it.
responses.response: We now agree on the shape of the citation. On B020, I would put the question to you directly: Spiering founded and led the AMANDA-era effort with Halzen and Karle, but members disagree on whether conception, construction or analysis deserves the credit, and the supplied text does not settle it. As long as that split is open I cannot support a three-name IceCube prize as a replacement for B030, even though I regard the neutrino window as a genuine discovery. I would be willing to look again if a clear, documented allocation emerged.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B022 but would not stand in the way of B030, regards B030 as his strongest alternative, and says he would defer to Lindroth and Kroll on technical priority questions.
responses.response: I appreciate the frankness about proximity, and I will repeat the technical judgement you asked about: the Katori and Ye allocation is defensible and the achievement is mature. On your own candidate, my reservation is about scope and not about merit. Car and Parrinello have the cleanest credit on the list, and I do not doubt the impact, but whether an ab initio simulation method is a physics invention or belongs with chemistry is a question the committee has not resolved, and your own colleagues in the opening ballots did not rank it. For me it stays below B030, B004 and B058, though I would not oppose its discussion.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the one-sentence distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I recall those citations from memory and have not checked them against the prize records.

Whether metrology experts would sustain the Katori and Ye pair against the contributions of Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow and the ion-clock groups; I would need a priority history of the first magic-wavelength lattice demonstrations to be sure.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should delay the award; I judge it should not, but I cannot rule out that some colleagues will treat it as a maturity argument.

If B030 were set aside, my first alternative is B004, with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller as my own trio, but I recognise that no B004 allocation is accepted by everyone and Esslinger's omission is a real cost.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My documented collaborators (L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Keller's group at ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) are not among the B030 names. I disclose general professional proximity to precision atomic physics and to ETH and Lund experimental groups, and I regard that as disclosure and not as a recusal-level conflict, but I leave it to the chair to decide. I do not judge B004 or B058 as lying in my own research area either, though B004 is near atomic physics.
